Director Makoto Shinkai

There is a question whispered at the start of our story:
How fast do cherry blossoms fall?

The answer: about five centimeters per second.

Just like the drifting petals, human hearts, too, can fall… softly, slowly, and sometimes apart.

This is the story of Takaki Tōno — a boy, a teenager, a man — whose life unfolds in three chapters.
A story of love, distance, and the gentle ache of time.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Have you ever dreamed of packing a single bag, hopping on a broomstick, and flying off to start a new life? Well, that's exactly what our hero, a young witch named Kiki, does in the enchanting story of Kiki's Delivery Service. According to witch tradition, at the age of 13, Kiki must leave her cozy home and find a new town to live in for a year, all on her own. With her talking black cat, Gigi, perched on her broom and her heart full of both excitement and a little bit of nervousness, she sets off into the vast night sky. They eventually discover the perfect spot, a bustling, beautiful port city by the sea named Kurik. The city is breathtaking, but starting a new life isn't as easy as it looks. Kiki feels a little out of place at first, but her luck changes when she meets Aono, the kind owner of a bakery. After Kiki uses her flying skills to return a pacifier to a customer, Osono offers her a room in exchange for helping out. This sparks a brilliant idea. Kiki decides to start her very own witch's delivery service. From delivering a stuffed cat toy to a little boy s birthday party to transporting a special herring and pumpkin pie baked by an elderly woman for her granddaughter, Kiki's business takes off. She soarses through the skies making deliveries and meeting all sorts of interesting people, including a friendly boy named Tombbo, who is obsessed with aviation and fascinated by her ability to fly. But it's not all clear skies. The pressures of work, the challenges of being independent, and a bout of self-doubt cause Kiki to experience something terrifying for a witch. She starts to lose her magic. Her broom becomes difficult to control, and she can no longer understand what Gigi is saying. This is the witch's version of an artist's block. A burnout that leaves her feeling lost and alone. Feeling discouraged, Kiki takes a break and visits her new friend, a forest dwelling artist named Ursula. Ursula shares her own experiences with creative slumps, explaining that inspiration and passion sometimes need a rest to recharge. She tells Kiki that magic, like art, comes from the heart. This advice comes at a crucial moment. A massive airship, a drift in a storm puts Tombbo's life in danger. Seeing her friend in peril, Kiki is faced with a choice. In a moment of sheer determination and courage, she grabs a simple street sweeper's broom, focuses with all her might and pours every ounce of her spirit into flying again. Her magic, shaky at first, returns in a powerful surge, allowing her to pull off a daring rescue in front of the whole city. Kiki becomes a celebrated local hero. She learns that magic isn't just about flying. It's about finding confidence, connecting with others, and believing in yourself, even when it's hard. She continues her delivery service now with a newfound maturity and joy, having truly found her place in the world. Thanks for watching. If you enjoyed this little trip into a world of magic and wonder, don't forget to like, share, and subscribe for more summaries.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en In the world of literature, few stories capture the essence of adolescence quite like Kiki's Delivery Service. This coming of age tale follows the journey of a young witch named Kiki, who after turning 13 sets off on a year-long journey to learn about the world and herself. Narrated by James Arnold Taylor and featuring enchanting music by Joe Husi, this animated film invites us into a world where magic intertwines with the everyday. So sit back, relax, and let's dive into this timeless tale. Welcome to our channel, your place for the best movie and book narration. One rainy afternoon in a quaint cottage surrounded by trees lived a young witch named Kiki. Kiki, a cheerful and determined girl, shared a close bond with her parents and her faithful black cat, Gigi. Their home was filled with laughter and the aroma of her mother's delicious potions. As Kiki turned 13 in a tradition loomed over the horizon, just like every young witch in her lineage, she was about to embark on a journey of self-discovery. Guided by her mother, Kiki prepared for her journey. Her mother, a skilled potion maker, presented her with a handmade broom as her companion. Meanwhile, her father, known for his warmth and gentle nature, gave her a comforting necklace. As the day of her departure arrived, the whole family gathered outside. Her father lifted her high in the air, reminding her that she would forever be his little girl. With a heart filled with excitement and a touch of nervousness, Kiki took off into the sky alongside Gigi. As they soared through the clouds, the wind tousling her hair, Kiki knew she was stepping into an adventure that would change her forever. After hours of flying, Kiki and Gigi came across a vast expanse of sparkling water. Below them, nestled between the sea and the land, lay a charming town buzzing with activity. Tramas clanged, shops beckoned, and the aroma of fresh bread drifted from nearby bakeries. Intrigued, Kiki decided to explore this vibrant town. Upon arriving, however, Kiki realized that being a witch in an ordinary town was not as simple as she had imagined. The town's people, curious and somewhat skeptical, eyed her curiously. While some greeted her with polite smiles, others openly questioned the relevance of witches in modern times. Despite the mixed reactions, Kiki remained determined to make the best of her situation. With no place to stay, no money, and no job, Kiki knew she had to take immediate action. Fortunately, fate intervened when she stumbled upon a kind woman named Osono, the owner of a local bakery. Recognizing Kiki's good heart, Osono took her in, providing her with food and shelter. In return, Kiki offered to help around the bakery, dusting shelves, kneading dough, and assisting in preparing the daily bread. Meanwhile, Gigi ever the pragmatist suggested that Kiki put her unique skills to use, offering delivery services using her broom. The idea sparked a light bulb moment in Kiki's mind. With that, she created signs advertising her new business, Kiki's delivery service. As news of her service spread, customers started trickling in. Kiki found joy in these deliveries. soaring through the sky and bringing smiles to people's faces. However, her success didn't come without its challenges. One day, while delivering a toy cat to a customer, Kiki encountered a sudden gust of wind, causing her to lose her balance. In a panic, she tried to regain control, but the package slipped from her grasp and fell into the forest below. Filled with remorse, Kiki immediately set out to retrieve the toy. As she searched, she came across a secluded cabin nestled amidst the trees. Gathering her courage, she knocked on the door. To her surprise, it was opened by a mysterious girl about her age with a kind smile and a hint of mischief in her eyes. The girl warmly welcomed her, offering her some tea and cookies. Kiki, feeling a sense of relief, explained her situation, apologizing for losing the toy. The girl, whose name was Ursula, listened patiently, and when Kiki left to continue her search, she went out to find the lost package herself. Moments later, she returned with the toy cats and with a gentle scolding for forgetting to secure it properly. Touching by his confession, Kiki responded with deep appreciation for his friendship, but also honesty about her evolving feelings. The party continued with laughter, music, and dancing, celebrating not just Kiki's journey, but the growth of the entire community. The next morning, with a heavy heart, but a sense of fulfillment, Kiki prepared for her journey home. As she stood before the bakery, ready to take off, Osano presented her with a beautifully decorated cake, symbolizing both her achievements and the sweet memories they had shared. Saying her goodbyes, Kiki soared into the sky, leaving behind the town that had become a second home to her. A tale of gods and monsters, betrayal, and the strength of a heart that refused to give up. This is the story of Hercules, the mighty son of Zeus, who fell from the heavens, rose from the ashes, and discovered what it truly means to be a hero. At the top of the majestic Mount Olympus, Zeus and Hia celebrate the birth of their son Hercules, a divine baby with godly strength. The gods rejoice and even the fate sing of his bright future. But not all share the joy. Far below in the underworld, the god of death, Hades broods plotting to overthrow Olympus. The fates reveal a prophecy. In 18 years, the planets will align, and if Hades unleashes the monstrous titans, he could seize power unless Hercules stands in his way. Fearful of the boy's growing strength, Hades hatches a dark plan. He sends his bumbling minions, pain, and panic to kidnap baby Hercules and feed him a potion to strip away his immortality. But the plan fails halfway. Hercules becomes mortal but retains his god-like strength. Taken in by a humble couple on Earth, Amphetrion and Alchemine, Hercules grows up feeling out of place to strong to clumsy to different. When he's a teenager, Hercules accidentally destroys a marketplace during one of his strength bursts. Confused and dismayed by his actions, he seeks answers. His adoptive parents finally tell him the truth and give him a medallion bearing the symbol of the gods. This leads Hercules to the temple of Zeus where a thunderous voice echoes from a giant statue. It is his father Zeus. Zeus reveals the truth. Hercules is his son. But because he drank the potion, he became mortal. There's only one way to return to Olympus. Become a true hero. to guide him. Hercules defeats it in a dazzling battle and overnight becomes a celebrity hero. Zero to hero. The crowds cheer, but fame is not the same as heroism. Enter Maggara, or Mag as she prefers. Smart, sarcastic, and fiercely independent, Mag is no damsel in distress. But unknown to Hercules, she's bound to Hades by a soul contract, forced to do his bidding. Hades sees an opportunity. If she helps him defeat Hercules, he'll free her from her contract. Torn between her freedom and her feelings, Mag reluctantly agrees. Hades tricks Hercules into giving up his strength for 24 hours in exchange for Mag's safety. With Hercules powerless, Hades unleashes the Titans. They storm Olympus in a climactic battle. The gods are overwhelmed. Meanwhile, a colossal cyclops heads toward thieves. Despite losing his strength, Hercules confronts it using only courage, cleverness, and grit. He defeats the giant, proving that heroism isn't about strength. It's about heart. But tragedy strikes. Me saves Hercules from falling debris and is fatally wounded. Her sacrifice breaks Hades contract and restores Hercules powers. Fueled by love and rage, Hercules rides Pegasus into the underworld. In Hades lair, Me's soul drifts toward the river of death. Without hesitation, Hercules dives into the river, willing to sacrifice his own life for hers. The river begins to drain his vitality. But just before he perishes, something miraculous happens. His selfless act transforms him. Hercules becomes a true hero. Not through battle, not through glory, but through sacrifice. The river rejects him. His godhood is restored. With his newfound power, he punches Hades into the sticks, rescues Meg, and soarses back to Olympus, a true god. The gods celebrate. Zeus offers him a place among them. But Hercules declines. His heart belongs on earth with Meg. Because in the end, being a hero means choosing love over immortality. Hercules may have been the son of Zeus, but he didn't need godly power to be a hero. All he needed was love. And let's face it, when has love ever been enough to solve everything? Let me explain. As a kid, we all grew up knowing the classic Disney stories, but sometimes those stories weren't exactly what they seemed. Disney took inspiration from the Brothers Grim, and if you know their stories, you'd know they weren't exactly kid-friendly. Disney also changed elements of the classic myths, like Hercules wasn't exactly known for his super chill attitude about being betrayed by his adoptive uncle. Even though this Disney version of Hercules shows how great it is to accept yourself, it can also teach us some pretty valuable lessons. When you think about it, Hercules story is a lot like a metaphor for puberty, which is why maybe it resonates with us so much. We all go through changes that we don't fully understand, feel like an outcast from society, and discover who we really are along the way. And there are deeper messages, too. Think about the message against greed. Remember that hydra that Hercules fought? Well, in Greek mythology, it represented the insatiable nature of evil. You see, as soon as you take something away, evil will always try to replace it, showing us that evil never stops coming until we do. But let's talk about those iconic songs. Music is such an important part of the Disney experience, and this movie is no exception. The music in Hercules reflects the character's emotions and moves the story forward. I won't say I'm in love is such an excellent example of this. It perfectly captures Me's internal conflict and adds layers to her character. But let's be honest, we all know the real star of the show is the villain. Hades is iconic. His charisma and comedic timing make him one of the greatest Disney villains of all time. His desire for power is understandable, making him more human and relatable. The song Hellfire showcases his inner turmoil, making us both fear and sympathize with him. Now, let's take a look at the amazing animation. Disney's attention to detail is mindblowing. From the backgrounds to the character designs, every frame is a masterpiece. The animation in fight scenes is breathtaking. The fluidity of motion is incredible. And let's not forget the visual gags. They're scattered throughout the movie, making it funnier and more enjoyable for everyone. The voice acting in Hercules is topnotch. Tate Donovan as Hercules. Kevin R. Nelson as the hilarious Phil, James Woods as the wonderfully wicked Hades, and Susan Egan as the voice of a true powerhouse, Meg. These voices brought these characters to life in a way that we couldn't imagine anyone else in those roles. Think about how Hercules uses foreshadowing. Throughout the film, the audience is given subtle hints and clues that contribute to the film's overall meaning. For example, the recurring motif of the medallion serves as a reminder of Hercules divine heritage and foreshadows his eventual return to Mount Olympus. Additionally, the use of motifs like the color red to symbolize courage and sacrifice further enhances the film s thematic depth. In conclusion, Disney's Hercules is more than just a fun-filled adventure. It's a coming of age story that tackles complex themes with humor and heart. The blend of classic storytelling, unforgettable characters, and stunning visuals creates an enchanting experience that continues to captivate audiences of all ages. So, the next time you hear the opening notes of Go the Distance, get ready to be transported to the mythical world of Hercules. Who knows, you might just discover new insights with each viewing. That's all for now, folks. Thanks for joining me on this epic journey through the story of Hercules. If you enjoyed this retelling, don't forget to give us a like and subscribe for more enchanting tales. Until next time, stay magical.

magic of Christmas and Santa.

“Around Christmas we spend a lot of time thinking about presents, but have you ever wondered why we give gifts? Learn about the life of Saint Nicholas and discover why he became known as one of the greatest giftgivers of all time.”
cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en It's beginning to look a lot like Christmas. The snow is falling, carols are playing, and the search for the perfect present is on. There's just something magical about Christmas, isn't there? The magic of Santa Claus in his flying sleigh, of children leaving out cookies for him and his reindeer, and of course, the magic of giving and receiving gifts. But have you ever stopped to think about the real reason behind the giving of Christmas presents? You probably associate gift giving with holidays like Christmas and birthdays. You may also associate it with other special occasions such as anniversaries, graduations, and weddings. But have you ever wondered why we give gifts? And how did Santa become known as one of the greatest gift givers of all time? To answer that question, we have to go back more than 1,500 years to a man named Nicholas. He was born in the year to 80 AD in the Greek city of Petara. His father was a wealthy landowner and his mother was a devout Christian. When Nicholas was still a young boy, his parents died and he inherited all of their wealth. Now instead of keeping the money for himself, he decided to give it away to those who had less. He gave food, clothing, and money to the poor and also purchase freedom for those who were enslaved. He was even known to sneak down from his bedroom window and drop bags of gold coins into the hands of sleeping beggars below. As the legend goes, one day he heard of a nearby king who wanted to marry off his three daughters. But the problem was that the king was too poor to provide dowies, which were very expensive gifts that had to be given to the king in order for him to marry his daughter. If he couldn't find the money for the dowies, his daughters would never be married and would likely die as a result. Upon hearing this, Nicholas took pity on the family and decided to help. He went to the king and offered to pay the dowy for each of his daughters. In secret, he put three bags of gold coins in sacks, snuck into the king<unk>s courtyard and dropped them down the chimney. The king s youngest daughter was the only one home at the time, and she saw the bags of gold land. at the foot of her stockings which were drying by the fire. When the stockings were later found filled to the brim with gold, the king was overjoyed. He knew that St. Nicholas had come to the rescue. And so it was that Nicholas became known as the patron saint of giving, the secret admirer, the quiet benefactor, the friend of children, and of course, Santa Claus. And that's why we give gifts at Christmas. Hey, thanks for watching. If you enjoyed this video, don't forget to click the like button and subscribe for more fun educational content. title: Mid Autumn Festival or the Moon Festival
fulltitle: Mid Autumn Festival or the Moon Festival
description:
The Mid Autumn Festival or the Moon Festival is a traditional Chinese holiday celebrated every year on the 15th day of the 8th month on the Chinese calendar.
This year it falls on September. It's a time for family reunions, just like Thanksgiving here in the States, but with a lunar twist.
The holiday is all about appreciating the beauty of the moon and giving thanks to the moon goddess Chang' e.
According to legend, Chang' e was an ordinary woman who was chosen to become the moon goddess after she accidentally drank an elixir that was meant for her husband, the Jade Emperor.
After she ascended to the moon, she was lonely and each year on this day, her husband would visit her and they would enjoy the reunion until, you know, he kicked her to the curb for good.
So, you know, the Jade Emperor, he's not really the nice guy you want to be stuck at home with.
Anyway, people celebrate the holiday by getting together with their families and eating mooncakes.
Mooncakes are delicious pastries filled with sweet or savory ingredients and they come in all shapes and sizes, just like the moon, which is said to be at its fullest and brightest on this night.
The round shape of the mooncakes symbolize the full moon and the reunion of families.
The most popular flavor is probably the lotus seed paste, but there's also bean, red bean, coconut, egg yolk, green tea and even durian.
You can also get really fancy ones like this five thousand dollar gold one that's actually edible. No joke.
Another fun thing about the holiday is the lantern riddles.
During the Lantern Festival, which takes place the day after the Moon Festival, people will set up elaborate lanterns
and then take turns trying to guess the riddles that are written on them.
Whoever guesses correctly gets to keep the lantern.
So if you're in China for this holiday, be sure to try some mooncakes and maybe even do a little lantern riddle guessing.
And if you can't be in China, then just stay up late and appreciate the moon from wherever you are.
Because even though we might be miles away from our loved ones, we can still come together and appreciate the beauty of the natural world.
Just don't stare too long at your phone. Put it down, look up and take in the view.
After all, that's what the moon goddess Chang'e would want us to do.
Thanks for watching and I'll see you next time.

We may start out scared, but if we approach things with an open mind and a little bit of courage, we can overcome our fears and find happiness.

And now that I'm an adult, I can buy all the cookie dough I want. So, I got two different kinds. One for me and one for my mom. We're going to make these cookies together because my mom is visiting this week. It's just nice to have some normaly, you know, like making cookies like we used to when we were kids. I think sometimes as we get older, we forget how to be kids. We forget how to have fun. And I really want to instill that in my son and also my mom to just have fun, laugh, and be silly. You know, life is tough. It's hard being an adult. So, I think it's important to have something to look forward to every week, something to bake, something to be grateful for. cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Hey, what's this? Oh, it's just my new favorite movie. It's called Nasaka of the Valley of the Wind. And let me tell you about it. On a dying planet that humans have poisoned with rampant industrialization, the last vestigages of civilization are locked in an eternal struggle over who will destroy the world first. In the far future, after World War II, humanity has decimated the environment and themselves with it. Giant insects rule the skies and the land is largely uninhabitable. But there is hope in the form of a mysterious valley untouched by war where nature is returning and the remnants of humanity live in peace. This valley, however, is surrounded by the toxic wastelands, a region so dangerous that no one dares cross it. The only exceptions are those cursed to wander the wasteland for the rest of their lives, like this guy. He's cursed because he did something bad in the past. And there Sauls to this woman who's cursed because she loves this man who cursed her to wander the wasteland for eternity. Ah, classic love story. Anyway, people from the valley go into the wasteland to look for rare plants so they can use them as medicine. And this time, one of the plants they re looking for is a cure for the valley's beloved leader, the pacifist princess Noika. Now, you may be asking yourself, why would a princess need a cure if she's already dead? Yeah, me too. See, Nazaka died 25 years ago while saving a baby bird that flew into her hair and got burned alive by her torch. She was resurrected by the gods, or at least some kind of weird magic mushrooms, though. So, now she lives on as an eternally 16-year-old child. Her people call her the warrior princess because she defends them against the giant bugs that fly out of the wasteland and attack the valley every year during the sea of decay when the winds carry toxic spores that make the bugs extra angry. She's a pacifist though, so she doesn't like killing bugs. And even though she's a princess, she doesn't really like being a ruler either. She'd much rather hang out with her best friends who are uh well, this guy who looks like an ooa and this other guy who looks like a furry mudkip. One day, a prince from a nearby nation shows up in the valley seeking asylum. His name is Ashitaka, and he's been cursed by a demon. If he stays in the valley, the curse will lift, but if he leaves, the curse will kill him. Everyone is very nice to him, especially Nasika, who finds him super cute. Meanwhile, a power-hungry general named Yupa is plotting to overthrow Nasake's father, the king, so he can conquer the valley and claim its fertile lands for his own militaristic nation, which, to be honest, probably wouldn't survive a week without the valley's abundant food supply. Yupa wants to force Nosaka into marriage with his dim-witted son so he can solidify his power, but she obviously says no. Then Yupa kidnaps her instead. Shitaka immediately sets off to rescue her, taking Noake's little sister Kushana along for the ride. Since she insists that she wants to save her big sis, soon enough, they run into some giant bugs. But instead of running away from them, Ashitaka decides to fight back, you know, because he's a prince and stuff. And to his surprise, Nasaka appears riding on top of a giant beetle, fighting off the others. Ashitaka and Nasaka reunite. They escape on a giant praying mantis, and then they decide to fly to a different country instead of going back to the valley. Turns out there's another human kingdom. Yay. But soon they're attacked by a giant mutated sea slug thing. As they flee, they crash land in the wasteland where they meet up with a group of scavengers. These guys live in a junkyard made entirely of old airplane parts and other junk that they use to make cool vehicles like this giant motorcycle. They also have this girl named Tetto who's mute, but also apparently a genius engineer. She's also been in love with this guy, the leader of the scavengers, for a long time, but he's too stupid to realize it. Classic romance. While staying with the scavengers, Ashitaka learns that the curse plaguing him is actually a side effect of the demon poison inside the slugs that roam the wasteland. This demon is sealed inside a giant crystal located in the center of the wasteland, deep within the sea of decay. And it turns out that the reason the bugs attack the valley every year is because the crystal radiation is making them all go crazy. Not good. Then while everyone is sleeping, Nasaka sneaks off to the sea of decay to try and purify the crystal herself. Ashitaka and the others find her and warn her that she'd die if she touches the crystal, but she ignores them and does it anyway. Turns out they were right. She does indeed die, but she comes back again. More plot armor. And she now realizes that the only way to defeat the demon inside the crystal is to accept it, embrace it, become one with it. She refuses to do this, though, because she believes in peace. And although she knows it'll probably kill her, she decides to try and purify the crystal once again. This time she is successful and the crystal returns to its original state, which means the sea of decay ends and the demon is sealed away once more. Unfortunately, this also causes all of the plants in the valley to suddenly die. Nasaka is devastated, but she is saved from total despair. When she discovers a single seed that has survived, she plants it and Ashitaka promises to protect it until it grows into a mighty tree. And now it's time for our final showdown. Yupa attacks Ashitaka and the others, but he's no match for a giant robot. Yeah, they pulled a giant robot out of nowhere. Don't ask. Theescu Masake's father shows up with an army to reclaim his daughter. But before anyone can stab anyone else, Nasika stops them and asks for forgiveness. She then reveals that she and Ashitaka have been secretly married. Double classic romance. And although she doesn't want to start a war, she's willing to defend her family and her friends if it comes down to it. Meanwhile, the scavengers have made a giant flying fortress out of the plane parts in their junkyard and are attacking Yupa's army with it. But just as the situation seems hopeless, Nazake's dad breaks through the enemy lines and kills Yupa. Then the movie ends. It's hard to overstate just how good Nazaka of the Valley of the Wind is. The animation is beautiful. The music is epic. The characters are unforgettable and the voice acting is superb. I mean, just listen to this. God, it's so good. It's basically perfect. But what makes Nasika truly great is its writing. The story is both thoughtprovoking and emotionally resonant, dealing with mature themes like environmentalism, pacifism, and the futility of war. For example, check out this speech Nasika gives to a group of children. It's one of the most powerful things I've ever heard in a movie. And yet, for all its intelligence, Nasika never feels preachy. The writing is so clever that it manages to simultaneously be both profound and entertaining. And I think that's what makes this movie so special. It's not just a kids movie, but it's not just a grown-up movie either. It's a movie for everyone. Oh, and did I mention it came out in 1984? Yeah, this movie is older than I am, and it still slaps. Well, that's all for today. Thank you so much for watching. And as always, remember to be kind to each

In the sprawling neon-drenched metropolis of Neotokyo, we follow a teenage biker gang member named Chitaaro Caneda living in a dystopian future where cybernetics and psychic abilities are commonplace. Chitaaro and his gang spend their days causing trouble and racing their motorcycles through the crowded streets. But their leisurely lifestyle comes to an abrupt end when one of Chitaaro's close friends, a young woman named Kai, is nearly killed by a mysterious government agent while on a routine motorcycle errand. Determined to get revenge, Chitaaro and his gang chase the agent through the chaotic streets of Neotokyo until they crash into a heavily guarded government facility known as the Gehern complex. And though they escape with their lives, Kai is left in a coma with a strange metallic object lodged in her head. Desperate to save his friend, Chitaaro visits an underground doctor who reveals that the only way to remove the object is with a powerful psychic, a rare breed of human with extraordinary mental abilities. But just as the operation is about to begin, Chitauro is confronted by the very agent who nearly killed Kai. And in a desperate attempt to protect his friend, he flees with the metallic object still lodged in her head, unaware that its removal was only temporary and that it would eventually return unless he could find a way to destroy it. As the story progresses, Chitaaro learns more about the nature of psychics and the true extent of the government's plans for them. It turns out that Kai was targeted because she possesses immense psychic power and the government wanted to use her as a weapon. But her powers are unstable and dangerous, causing massive explosions whenever she uses them. Determined to save Kai and prevent the government from exploiting her powers, Chitauro joins forces with a group of psychics led by a mysterious figure known only as Titsuo. But as Chitaaro becomes more involved with the psychics, he begins to lose control over his own humanity, turning into a rampaging psychic psychopath who goes on a murderous rampage through Neotokyo, slaughtering anyone who gets in his way. It's up to his best friend, Kaneda, to stop him before he destroys everything and everyone they love. And it's not easy. As the two friends fight, Chitaaro's psychic powers grow stronger, turning him into a terrifying monster with the ability to control minds, alter reality, and even bring people back from the dead. But Keda refuses to give up, knowing that his friend is still in there somewhere. And eventually he's able to break through to Chitauro, reminding him of the good times they shared and the people who love him, bringing him back from the brink and ending the threat he poses to Neotokyo. In the aftermath, Canada and the remaining psychics work together to rebuild the city and atone for the damage that espin. And though they may never fully understand the true extent of their powers, they know that they must use them responsibly to protect the world from the dangers that lie ahead. The animation in Akira is truly something to behold, especially for a movie that came out in 1988. The filmmakers created a unique style that blends traditional handdrawn animation with computerenerated imagery, resulting in a visual feast of neon lights, high-speed motorcycle chases, and explosive action sequences. But the movie isn't just a mindless action flick. It tackles some serious themes like government corruption, the dangers of unchecked power, and the importance of friendship and redemption. The characters may be flawed and sometimes even unlikable, but they re also incredibly human and their struggles and sacrifices are all the more powerful because of it. If you re a fan of anime movies like Ghost in the Shell or The Boy and the Beast, then chances are you'll love Akira. Just be prepared for a wild ride that will leave you questioning the nature of humanity, the power of friendship, and the true meaning of sacrifice. Thanks for watching.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en Freedom is something that we all want in life, but most of us don't really know what it means to be free. We think that freedom means being able to do whatever we want, whenever we want, whenever we feel like it. But true freedom is so much more than that. When you look at a bird that's sitting on a tree, do you think the bird is free? Well, of course it is. It's free to fly wherever it wants to, right? Wrong. You see, that bird is trapped by its circumstances. It doesn't have the freedom to do what it really wants to do because it's chained to that tree by its own past experiences. Because that bird has been captured and caged many times in the past, it now lives in fear. So even though it may appear to be free, it's not. True freedom means not being chained to anything, not being held back by anything or anyone, and not being afraid of anything. And that bird certainly is afraid of something. So, you may be wondering, how can I be truly free? Well, the first step towards freedom is to become aware of what's holding you back. Are you holding on to some old grudges or past hurts? Are you afraid of what others think of you? These are the things that are holding you back from being truly free. The second step towards freedom is to let go of the things that are holding you back. This doesn't mean that you should just forget about those things or pretend that they never happened. It means that you need to acknowledge them, accept them for what they are, and then let them go. When you do this, you'll start to feel a sense of peace and calm that you've never felt before. And with that, you will also start to feel more confident and self assured. The third step towards freedom is to start living your life according to your own values and principles. When you do this, you'll start to feel like you're in control of your life and that you're no longer being controlled by external circumstances or the opinions of others. You see, freedom is not something that you find. It's something that you create for yourself. It's a way of living that you choose to live. So if you want to be truly free, then make the choice today to let go of the things that are holding you back and start living your life according to your own values and principles. Do this and you will find that you are more free than you ever thought possible.

There was a poor but good little girl who lived alone with her mother, and they no longer had anything to eat. Today we're looking at Neon Genesis Evangelion, the end of Evangelion, the concurrent theatrical ending of the TV series Neon Genesis Evangelian. This movie was released in 1997. This movie is not a recap. If you want to watch the series first, I would highly recommend that. And if you have watched the series, this movie picks up immediately after the events of episode 24. There are no real spoilers here since this movie is technically part of the show. So, let's get right into it. The movie begins with Shinji, Rey, and Asuka trapped inside the belly of the giant Ava unit Z01. The three of them are rescued by Kawaru, who had previously been put into a catatonic state by Seal. With Kawaru's help, Shinji repairs the damage to Ava Zo1 and they all escape from the collapsing HQ building of Nerve. They are then picked up by Misato and Ritsuko in a submarine where everyone begins to argue about what to do next. In the middle of the argument, Shinji begins to feel unwell and he along with the other two avers is suddenly compelled to dive deep into the ocean. They reach a trench over 7 mi deep and find an enormous black sphere. As Shinji and the others approach the sphere, their bodies begin to break down and they revert to their previous forms, stripped of all their memories and knowledge. We then cut to a flashback where we see that Gendo had been working with Seal the entire time after the events of episode 24. He reveals to them the true form of the human instrumentality project. His plan was to use the core of Adam which he had sealed within himself and the core of Lilith which was sealed within Ever01. To initiate the project, he explains that it is not the angels that are the enemy but the human race itself. He believes that the only way for humanity to evolve is through total extinction and rebirth. In the present, Shinji, Rey, and Asca are now infants once again. Jendo makes his way to the beach where the giant Ava01 is. He enters the Ava and prepares to merge with the core of Lilith. He is confronted by Yui, the mother of Shinji and the previous pilot of Ava01. She reveals that she has been sealed within the Eva the entire time and begs Jendo to stop his plan. Jendo refuses saying that humanity has already caused enough suffering and death. He initiates the instrumentality project and the entire world is consumed by the core of Lilith. We then cut to a flashback where we see that Yui had actually been dead the whole time and her consciousness had been uploaded to the internet dimension. In the present, Jendo and Yui's consciousness meet in the middle of the human sea. Jendo apologizes to Yui for everything and admits that he was wrong. The two of them share a kiss and then they are both consumed by light. In the final scene, Shinji, Rey, and Asuka are seen playing on a beach. The movie ends without any dialogue, and all we can really do is infer that they have all regained their memories and humanity has been given a second chance. So, this movie is pretty insane. It definitely deserves its reputation as one of the most mind-bending anime movies ever made. There are so many twists and turns that I couldn't possibly go into here. You just have to watch it for yourself. If you enjoyed this video, please leave a like and comment below to let me know your thoughts. I'll be watching the series again and then making a fulllength video essay on this movie, so make sure to stay tuned for more updates. Thanks for watching and I'll see you next time.

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en In feudal Japan, a young Amishi prince named Ashitaka is adored by his village for his strength and skill with the bow. But his life changes dramatically when he kills a mysterious boar. The beast is cursed, having been transformed by the vengeful spirit of the forest into a raging demon. In its final moments, it transfers that curse onto Ashitaka. Unless he can find a way to break the curse before it consumes him, he will become a mindless killing machine like the demon boore. So Ashitaka sets out on a journey to find a cure. And he soon finds himself at the gates of Iron Town, an enormous settlement of humans deep in the forest. For centuries, the settlement's iron works have flourished thanks to the hard work of the town's people and the mystical guidance of their leader, Lady Aboshi. That is until recently when the forest itself has begun fighting back against the relentless expansion of Iron Town. Giant predatory plants suddenly attack travelers. Mysterious diseases ravage the town's cattle, and wolves begin hunting men. The town's people fear that the forest itself is come to devour them all. But for Ashitaka, these are just the first signs of a much greater threat. As he ventures further into the forest, he encounters giant animals unlike anything he's ever seen before. But they are not beasts, nor are they spirits. Instead, they are human, cursed, and mutated by the forest power. Worse yet, the biggest and most terrifying of the lot is none other than the demon boar that Ashitaka killed. Now more powerful than ever, consumed by the forest's energy. And so Ashitaka's search for a cure, becomes a race against time to save himself from becoming a mindless monster. Meanwhile, he has stumbled into the middle of an even greater conflict between the humans of Iron Town and the forest itself, personified by the wolf princess Monoke. Will Ashitaka help the humans or the spirits win this war? Or will he be consumed by the curse before he can make a choice? Now, if you haven't already guessed, this is going to be a Princess Monokei appreciation video. So, if you have any requests for topics you would like me to cover in the future, please let me know in the comments below. The next entry in our ranking of Studio Gibli films, begins with one of the best opening sequences in any film, period. We open on a snowy village nestled deep within a primeval forest. It's the domain of the great forest spirit, also known as Morrow, mother of the forest. Her wisdom is revered throughout the ancient woodlands, but she is rarely seen by the creatures that live there. Deep within her domain, a young wolf gives birth to a baby girl and immediately runs off, presumably to be hunted by wolves. No, wait, wrong movie. Anyway, as the baby girl lays helpless in the snow, a massive boar charges through the trees and promptly adopts her as his own. Years pass and the boar is found dead, impaled by Ashitaka's arrow. But as he delivers the killing blow, the dying boar transfers a dark curse onto Ashitaka. A curse that will transform the young prince into a monstrous demon boore if he doesn't find a cure in time. This cold open accomplishes several things. First, we learn that the great forest has a spirit, Morrow. Second, we learn about the bond between the forest and the wolves who seem to be her children. Third, we learn that this world is brimming with magic. Finally, we meet Ashitaka and get an early glimpse of his compassion and skill as a warrior. Over the next few minutes, we're introduced to his family and friends, and we see how much they love and respect him. So when he learns about the curse, we care about him and want him to find a cure. And then his friends, well, they want to help, too. But they know there's no cure for a curse laid upon by a demon. And so Ashitaka is forced to leave his friends behind and seek out the source of the curse. Now, while the pacing here might feel slow compared to modern standards, this is actually pretty typical for a Japanese animated film, which tend to take their time getting to the good stuff. And trust me, once we get to Iron Town, the movie does not waste any time ramping up the action and suspense. We are quickly introduced to Lady Aboshi, the enigmatic leader of Iron Town and San aka Princess Moninoki, a feral child raised by wolves who considers herself to be more wolf than human. Then we are treated to one of the best action scenes in any studio Gibli film. A massive battle between the humans of Iron Town and the animals of the forest. And then right when you think it's over, bam, another massive battle, this time between the spirits of the forest and Ashitaka himself. In fact, some of the action scenes in Princess Moninoki are genuinely breathtaking. There's something incredibly exciting about watching a massive boar charge through the forest, crashing through trees, and sending birds scattering. And even though the film is almost 2 hours long, the pacing never feels slow. Miyazaki keeps us constantly on the edge of our seats, wondering just what Ashitaka will do next. When it comes to the animation, well, if you've seen any other Studio Giblly films, you'll know what to expect. gorgeous handdrawn animation filled with incredible attention to detail and some of the best color palettes you'll ever see. In fact, Princess Monoke is often cited as being one of the best animated films ever made because of its unique animation style and its mature storytelling. For example, notice how the backgrounds are almost always perfectly symmetrical, giving the characters plenty of room to move around in, or how the colors shift depending on whether we're watching a scene through Ashitaka's eyes or someone else's. It's these little touches that elevate Princess Monoke above your typical animated film and firmly establish it as a masterpiece. That is not to say that the voice acting in the English dub is particularly memorable. I mean, Claire Danes does a decent job as the voice of Moninoi, but the rest of the cast, not so much. However, I can't say for sure whether the English dub is bad or if it's just because I'm used to hearing these characters in Japanese. Either way, if you have the option to watch the film in Japanese with subtitles, I would recommend doing that. But regardless of the language, the voice acting is good enough to get the job done. And really, that's all you can ask for from a voice actor. One thing that I think could have been improved, however, is the film's ending. Now, don't get me wrong. It's a satisfying conclusion that ties up all of the loose ends and leaves us with a nice message about humanity and nature, but it just feels a bit rushed compared to the rest of the movie. I would have liked to see a few more scenes showing Ashitaka and Monoke's relationship develop before they decided to settle down and have kids. Still, it's a small gripe for what is otherwise a fantastic film, and it does give us one of the cutest babies in any studio Giblly film. Overall, Princess Moninoi is everything I could have asked for in a fantasy adventure. An epic story with unforgettable characters, beautiful animation, excellent voice acting, and themes that still resonate today. It's no wonder why Princess Moninoi is widely regarded as one of the greatest animated films ever made, and it's definitely my favorite Studio Gibli film. What about you guys? Let me know in the comments below. If you enjoyed this video, please hit the like button and subscribe. If you want to see more videos like this in the future, you can follow me on social media or check out my website. Thank you so much for watching and I'll see you next

cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en This is Spirited Away, the highest grossing anime film of all time. It's about a sullen 10-year-old girl who moves with her parents to the suburbs. One day, while exploring their new neighborhood, she wanders into a world ruled by gods, witches, and spirits, and where humans are changed into beasts. It's up to her to find a way to save her parents and everyone else who's been taken. But how? Well, she'll have to get a job from the witch Huba, who runs a bath house that caters to these spirits. The only problem is she doesn't want to bathe dirty spirits for a living. Oh, and also, she can't die, or else she'll be trapped there forever. And if that wasn't enough, she also has to avoid this creepy demon thing that stalks her everywhere she goes. So, yeah, this movie is like an hour and a half of non-stop plot. The story is so crazy that it feels like a fever dream. Like one minute our protagonist is walking through the woods and the next she is naked and covered in mud. And then later she's working in a bath house full of weird customers. And then later she's trying to avoid a giant demon baby while riding on the back of a giant flying fish. Now, even though it's fast-paced and action-packed, the movie isn't without its slow moments, there are some beautifully animated sequences, like when Chihiro first enters the spirit world, and we get this gorgeous pan shot that takes us from the forest to the river to the sky. These slow moments help make the movie feel epic. It's not just some random things happening. There's a clear progression to the story. But what makes Spirited Away special aren't the visuals or the plot, it's the characters. From the very beginning, we see that Chihiro isn't a normal 10-year-old girl. When her family moves to the suburbs, she misses her friends and feels isolated. She doesn't want to explore their new neighborhood because she's too busy sulking and eating snacks. She doesn't really change or grow throughout the story, but at least she doesn't have to. The movie is about her learning to appreciate the people around her, not about becoming a better person. When she first starts working at the bath house, she's rude and lazy. She does not want to do any work, and she gets upset when the spirits do not tip her. But over time, we see her slowly open up and become more friendly. We get some great character development for a movie that's only 127 minutes long. I mean, there's Haku, the mysterious spirit that helps Chihiro throughout the movie. At first, he's cold and distant, but as Chihiro gets to know him, we learn that he's actually really sweet and caring. And then there's no face, the lonely spirit who becomes obsessed with Chihiro. He's one of the most tragic characters in the movie, and his arc is both heartbreaking and thoughtprovoking. The voice acting is fantastic. Roomi Hiagi does a great job voicing Chihiro. She makes us feel the character's pain and frustration. And then there's Mamoru Myano who voices Haku. His voice is so soothing and calming. It's perfect for the character. But no voice actor steals the show like Tekashi Nau who voices no face. His voice is so expressive. You can tell exactly how he's feeling just from listening to him. Whether he's being kind or cruel, lonely or angry, Nedo conveys all of his emotions perfectly. There are so many amazing voice actors in this movie, and they all come together to create something truly special. But what about the music? Well, Joe Hisayishi delivers an Oscar-winning score that perfectly compliments the visuals. The soundtrack is a mix of orchestral and traditional Japanese instruments, and it sets the tone for each scene perfectly. But what about the animation? Well, let me tell you, Studio Gibli knocked it out of the park. The animation is gorgeous. The movie was clearly made with a lot of love and care, and it shows. From the smallest details to the biggest action sequences, everything is just so well done. Overall, Spirited Away is an amazing movie. It's beautifully animated, has a great story, and unforgettable characters. It's no wonder why it's the highest grossing anime film of all time.

title: Tale of Two Witches
description:
Once upon a time in a spooky old house on a dark and stormy night, there lived a kind witch named Hazel.
She brewed magical potions and cast delightful spells, spreading joy throughout the neighborhood.
But alas, her sister, the dreadful Griselda, practiced wicked witchcraft and longed to rule the town with an iron fist.
Now, despite their differences, they shared one thing in common, a deep love for cats.
And when a lost kitten meowed pitifully on their doorstep, Hazel took it in without hesitation.
But Griselda, with her heart as cold as a witch's cauldron, flung the poor creature out into the storm.
"A witch's house is no place for a stray," she cackled.
"Quick, get out of here before I turn you into a toad."
However, something remarkable happened.
Instead of cowering in fear, the kitten stood its ground, arched its back and let out a mighty roar that shook the very foundations of the house.
Startled by this unexpected display of bravery, Griselda retreated into her room, leaving Hazel to care for the kitten.
As the days passed, the kitten grew stronger and more courageous, and Hazel couldn't help but feel a sense of pride.
She named him Midnight and taught him how to fish for compliments with a magic wand and yarn ball.
Together, they explored the enchanting Whispering Woods, where trees gossiped secrets and flowers bloomed in every color imaginable.
Meanwhile, Griselda seethed with envy, watching from afar as Hazel and Midnight became the talk of the town.
"That wretched cat has brought nothing but chaos to my peaceful home," she grumbled.
"I must do something drastic before my cauldron bubbles over with rage."
And so the wicked witch concocted a wicked plan.
She transformed herself into a beautiful white dove and flew to the village, where she cast a spell on the baker, causing him to fall madly in love with the first person he laid eyes on, which, ugh, just happened to be Griselda.
Then she repeated the process with the cobbler, the tailor and every eligible bachelor in town until she had an entire army of lovestruck men at her command.
With their help, she marched on Hazel's house, determined to put an end to her sister's happiness once and for all.
But little did she know that Midnight had overheard her plans and had already alerted his fairy godmother, the great and powerful Luna.
As Griselda's goons approached the house, Luna swooped down from the sky, transforming Midnight into a magnificent lion with a flick of her magic wand.
Startled by the sudden appearance of a real life Disney character, the men froze in their tracks.
Then, with a deafening roar, the lion pounced, sending them running for their lives.
Griselda, however, was not so easily defeated. She raised her hands and unleashed a torrent of dark magic, but Luna was unfazed.
With a wave of her wand, she banished Griselda's spells and sent her tumbling into her own cauldron.
"It's over, Griselda," Luna boomed. "Your reign of terror ends today."
But before she could finish the job, a tiny meow interrupted her.
Startled, Luna turned and saw Hazel standing before her, holding a small, familiar looking kitten in her arms.
"Please, Great Luna," Hazel pleaded. "My sister may be misguided, but she's still my family.
I beg you, spare her life and turn her into a cat instead."
Touched by Hazel's compassion, Luna agreed. And with a wave of her magic wand, Griselda was transformed into a fluffy grey tabby cat.
As the townspeople looked on, Hazel and Griselda embraced, realizing that love and kindness were far more powerful than any curse or spell.
They lived happily ever after, or at least until next week's episode.

Instead, it invites players to engage with these themes on a deeper level, encouraging empathy and understanding. From that drop of sunlight, a magic flower grew, which had the power to heal the sick and wounded. An old woman named Mother Gothol selfishly kept the flower hidden and used its magic to keep herself young and beautiful for many years. In a nearby kingdom, the queen was about to have a baby, but she grew very ill. The people went out in search of the miraculous golden flower of legend in hopes that it would heal their queen. They found the flower and scooped it out of the ground. They used it to make a medicine that healed the queen and she gave birth to a beautiful baby girl with shining golden hair. They named her Rapunzel. Mother Gothol was angry that the flower was taken from her, so she snuck into the palace. She realized that Rapunzel's golden hair held the power of the magic flower. So, she tried to cut some. But when the hair was cut, it turned brown and lost its power. Mother Gothal had no choice but to take the whole child. She stole Rapunzel and hid her away in a tall tower in the forest. The king and queen were distraught that they couldn't find her. So every year on her birthday, the kingdom lit floating lanterns and flew them into the sky in hopes that one day Rapunzel would find her way home. Rapunzel grew up thinking Mother Gothol was her real mom and Mother Gothol told her lies about how awful and cruel the outside world was to make Rapunzel afraid of leaving the tower. But still, Rapunzel grew up a kind and curious child. Every year on her birthday, she snuck out of her room to look out the tower window and watched as lights floated up into the sky. She wondered what they were and wanted to go see them up close. "Take me to see the floating lights and return me here safely," she said. In return, she would give Flynn back the satchel with the crown, which she'd hidden under some floorboards. He reluctantly agreed. The world outside her tower was wondrous, and Rapunzel loved everything about it, but she was still a bit frightened of it. Flynn thought he could scare Rapunzel into giving up her quest and get his satchel back quicker, so he brought her to the Snuggly Duckling, a tavern filled with ruffians and thugs. Rapunzel was afraid at first, but she was kind-hearted and compassionate. She found that she had something in common with all of those big, burly, scary men. They all had a dream. When the palace guards came, they ran down a tunnel and Rapunzel used her hair to swing herself and Flynn to safety. But they ended up trapped in a cave that was flooding with water. Rapunzel used her magic hair to light the darkness and find a way to escape. Flynn was amazed that her hair magically glowed. "It doesn't just glow," Rapunzel said. She then used her hair to heal a cut on his hand. Meanwhile, the Stabington brothers met up with Mother Gothol, who'd realized Rapunzel had left the tower, and they chased after Flynn and Rapunzel together. Mother Gothol tried convincing Rapunzel that Flynn only wanted the crown and didn't actually care about her. She dared Rapunzel to return it to him and see what happened. Then she left. Maximus the horse caught up with Flynn and Rapunzel. But Rapunzel convinced him to let Flynn show her the lights first. Then they could chase each other to their hearts content. Flynn then showed Rapunzel around the kingdom. Some girls braided her hair with flowers so it wouldn't get tangled up everywhere, and Flynn thought she looked beautiful. He took her to read books in a library. They ate cupcakes, and she drew a beautiful mural with chalk. When it was time to go watch the lights, Flynn took Rapunzel out on the water in a little boat. Flynn had gotten them lanterns to light, too. And they watched them soar up into the sky, lighting up the night like stars. Rapunzel gave him back the satchel with the crown because she trusted he wouldn't abandon her. But Flynn realized he didn't want riches anymore. He just wanted to be with Rapunzel. He put down the satchel and took her hands. But before they could kiss, Flynn saw the Stabington brothers appear on the shore. "I'll be right back," he promised Rapunzel and left her on shore with the boat. He took the satchel and went to meet the brothers. He tried giving them back the crown so they'd leave him alone, but Mother Gothol had told them about Rapunzel's magic hair, and they decided they wanted her instead. So they tied Flynn up on a boat and sent him across the water to be arrested by the guards. They went after Rapunzel, but Mother Gothol jumped in and stopped them. She wanted Rapunzel to think she'd saved her, when really she'd been the one to send the brothers after Rapunzel in the first place. Rapunzel, thinking Flynn had betrayed her, went back to the tower with Mother Gothol. In the jail, Flynn saw the Stabington brothers in another cell. He grabbed them through the bars. "What did you do to her?" he demanded. "It wasn't us," they said. "It was the old lady." Flynn realized Mother Gothol was behind the whole thing, and Rapunzel was in danger. Luckily, Maximus had gone back to the snuggly duckling and got Rapunzel's new thug friends to come help Flynn escape. Flynn rode Maximus through the forest and climbed the tower. Once inside, he saw Rapunzel tied up in the corner and Mother Gothol stabbed him from behind. Mother Gothal tried pulling Rapunzel out the back door, but she struggled and fought. Stop fighting, Rapunzel. No, Rapunzel said, "I will never stop fighting to get away from you. But if you let me heal him, I will go with you. I won't ever try to escape. I promise. Just let me heal him." Mother Gothol agreed. She tied Flynn up so he wouldn't follow them and Rapunzel went to heal him, but Flynn stopped her. He knew if she went with Mother Gothol, she'd be unhappy for the rest of her life. So Flynn took a shard of a broken mirror and cut off all her magic hair. That way, Mother Gothal couldn't use Rapunzel and keep her prisoner. Without the magic, Mother Gothol turned to dust. Rapunzel's hair lost its golden color and turned brown. And she couldn't heal Flynn. She bent her head and cried, singing her magic song. But even without her hair, Rapunzel still had magic in her. cleaned_subtitles: Kind: captions Language: en The Amazing Gazelle. Zanzibar is an island in the deep blue Indian Ocean just off the coast of East Africa. If you stand in the port of Zanzibar and look out to sea, you can watch the small speedy sailing boats called Dows used by traders and fishermen for centuries past. Explore the winding streets and you will find stone houses, intricately carved doors, bustling markets, and lazy terraces. Five times a day, the loudspeakers attached to the minouetses of the mosques broadcast the call to prayer for the faithful followers of Islam. For several hundred years, Zanzibar was ruled by Arabs from the Sultenate of Omen. The Arab traders dealt in crops, ivory, spices, and slaves. The common language of Zanzibar and much of East Africa is Swahili, which includes African, Arabic, and European influences. You might have heard some Swahili words in films such as The Lion King. For instance, Simba is a lion. Jambo means hello and Hakuna matata means no problem. The fables from Zanzibar are a mixture of African and Arabic tales. You will hear about Arabic sultans and African people and talking animals. They often celebrate clever and cunning tricks too. There was once a beggar whose name was Alamani. Every day he would go to the village rubbish heap and scratch around for scraps of food. His search was hard because all the poor villagers were careful about what they threw away. Sometimes he would find no more than a few grains and seeds. One day something glinted in the morning sun. His sharp eyes did not miss this sign of good luck. He stooped down and picked up a silver coin known as a piece of eight. His stomach said to him, "Go to the market and buy food for a fine meal." But his head replied, "No, stomach. You will be satisfied today, but tomorrow you will be even more bitter in your hunger. Best keep this coin until something special comes along." A few days later, a traitor came along the grassy track to the village. His donkey pulled a cage made of twigs, in which sat a gentle creature with big dough eyes and long pointy horns. She was a gazelle, an African deer, and a by word for grace and loveliness. Alhamdani saw the animal and thought, "Here is a beauty I would like to possess." And he called out to the traitor, "Friend, stop for a while so that I may examine your wares." The other villagers laughed and scorned. "That beggar has no money to buy gazels," they said. "He gets his food by scratching like a hen in the dust heap. Go near him at your peril. He will pick your purse." But the traitor replied, "I have seen well-dressed men who demand my price, and when I tell them, they say, "Why your gazels are too expensive for us? Perhaps he who wears rags will consider my animals to be a bargain, God willing. The traitor was rewarded for his open mind when Al Hamdani reached into his torn and dusty clothes and pulled out a silver piece of eight. He took a small gazelle out of the cage and handed it to the beggar, saying, "Here, master, take this one. I call it kijupa." Then turning to the villages, he laughed and said, "You with your white robes and turbans and swords and daggers and sandals on your feet. You gentlemen of property, you told me this man was too poor to buy anything. Yet he has bought a gazelle for a silver coin." Alhamdani beamed a smile of yellow teeth and happily led the gazelle back to his hut. That night they slept together on the straw and in the morning they went out to the dust heap to look for morsels to eat. The following night when it was dark and they were alone together in the hut. A low voice whispered. Master Alhamdani sat up with a start and said, "Who's that?" "It is I," said the voice. "Your faithful gazelle Kajipa." At this the beggar was more surprised than ever. He did not expect the gazelle to talk. "What wonder is this?" he asked. "No cause for any amazement at all," said Kijapa. "Do I wonder that you can talk?" Then she explained why she had woken up her master. "I am grateful to you, my master, because you spent your last penny to buy me and to release me from the cage of twigs. But to tell you the truth, I cannot sleep because I am so hungry. Let me go free in the morning to search for my own food and in the evening I promised to return to you. Alhamdani blinked and pinched himself to see if he was dreaming. It seemed that he was awake and he agreed to let the amazing gazelle do as she asked. In the morning she went out to forage for food. All day he freted and worried if he would ever see his beautiful pet again. But in the evening she faithfully returned to him. The following morning she went out again to find her own food. And the day after, and indeed every day, until on the fifth day, she put a pore on a clot of earth, turned it over, and found something hard and shiny. This is nothing other than a diamond. She said to herself, "When I give it to my master, he will be rich, and all his troubles will be at an end." She picked up the diamond in her soft mouth and headed for home. But as she went along, she thought, "But for how long will he be rich? The other villagers will surely accuse him of stealing the precious stone and will take it off him." And having thought this over, she devised another plan. The amazing gazelle turned around and headed along the road for the Sultan's palace. When she arrived at the gates, she spoke to the guards saying, "I have brought a valuable gift for his excellency." The gods were so surprised to hear the animals speak that they said, "Indeed, this is a wonder for our master to behold, and they brought Kipper before the sultan." The gazelle went down on her knees before the great ruler and dropped the diamond at his feet. Your Majesty, this is a gift from my master who is as wealthy as he is wise. His name is Alhamdani and he sends this as a token of his good faith. He wishes to unite two noble families. The Sultan understood this to mean that Alhamdani wished to marry his daughter. He thought himself, "A man who sends a talking gazelle with a diamond as a gift would indeed make a worthy relative." He spoke aloud to the remarkable visitor saying, "Arise and return to your master. Tell him the sultan wishes his presence at the palace to celebrate the wedding of his eldest princess and Alhamdani." The gazelle had been away some time, and his master had been overcome with grief. The villagers mocked him, saying, "See how the dirt scratcher has lost his one piece of good fortune. Even his precious gazelle has run away from him. But that night, as Alhamdany lay asleep, he felt a soft nose nudging his face, he turned round and saw in the moonlight that his graceful companion had returned. Now listen carefully, said the gazelle. I bring you good news. Do not ask what it is. Just do everything exactly as I say, and you will not regret it. The beggar nodded and felt no fear about agreeing to do anything he was told. Because the good thing about having nothing is that you have nothing to lose. At first light, the beggar and the animal set off along the dusty road. They walked all day and towards evening. When they came to a stream, the gazelle said, "Lie down here in the ditch by the water, and do not move." Alhamdani did exactly as he was told and lay still while the deer kicked and pummeled him with her claws until he was bruised and scratched all over. Then she ordered him to stay exactly where he was until she returned. She took off on her heels down the road, kicking up the dust behind her. When she reached the palace, she demanded to see the sultan immediately and declared, "My master has been attacked by robbers and lies bruised and beaten by the road. They have taken his robes and all the finery he brought for the wedding." On hearing this dreadful news, the sultan sent his attendants to search for Al Hamani where he lay by the stream. When they found the poor man, they revived him with smelling salts, gave him food and water, washed his wounds, bathed him in the stream, and dressed him in robes of silk. In this way, the beggar arrived at the palace, dressed for his wedding as a prince. As soon as the wedding was complete, the faithful gazelle went off in search for a fitting home for her newly married master. She ran along the road until she came to large stone house with emeralds and precious stones encrusted around the windows and doors. "Here's the place," she said to herself before knocking on the door. She knocked and nobody answered. She knocked again and nobody answered. She knocked a third time and an old serving woman opened the door. The gazelle said, "Good lady, I wish to speak to the master of the house." The old woman did not look surprised at all to see an animal talk. Instead, she said, "Be gone with you, unless you long for your own death." "First pray, tell me who the master of this house is," insisted the gazelle. "He is a wicked seven-headed serpent. He has killed the rightful owner, and he will surely do for you if he returns and finds you here. Is there a good sword in the house? asked the gazelle. The old woman said that there surely was. Then lend it to me, and I shall deal with the serpent. A little while later, there was a sound like the approach of a great storm. Dust, brushwood, and debris began to blow down the street. Prepare to meet your doom," said the woman. "We'll see about that," said the gazelle. She took up position just inside the house, holding the sword between her paws. When the great snake arrived, he smelt something unusual, and said to the old lady, "What is this new meat you have prepared for me?" And she replied, "It is delicious. Why don't you pop inside and try it?" The serpent poked one of his seven heads through the doors. And as he did so, the gazelle brought the sword down and sliced it off. The cut was so clean that the monster felt nothing more than a tickle. He put his second head inside, and the gazelle sliced that one off, too. "Who scratched me?" demanded the snake. "It was I, Kijipper," replied the gazelle. The serpent was curious to see who Kijapa might be and put his third head through the door. This too was cut off. And so it continued until all seven of his heads had been removed and he was dead. The old lady rejoiced and Kjippa went to fetch her master and his bride. In the meantime, the servants of the former master returned and made the beautiful house ready for them. And so the happy couple had every luxury and comfort that they could desire. But it did not take long for Alhamdani to forget his former poverty. If he was lazy before, he was more lazy now. He grew fat and arrogant and forgot to thank his faithful gazelle. One day, Kijijipper said sadly to the old woman, "I have arranged for Alhamdani who was formerly a beggar to marry the daughter of a sultan and to move into a fine house with servants. And the strangest thing is he has not once asked me how I did any of this for him." Not long after that, Kijipper became ill and took to her bed. The old lady went to see Alhamdani and said, "Master, your gazelle is sick and aches all over." Alhamdani replied, "What do I, a man of wealth and position, care about an animal that cost a single silver coin? Give her some grl and tell her she is fortunate to live in this house." The old woman was shocked to hear of his lack of concern for the faithful animal. Soon Kjipper grew worse and Alhamdani's young wife came to plead on behalf of the gazelle. My husband Kjipper is growing worse and her groans are terrible to hear. Alhamdani replied. Then stuff up your ears with wax. Soon after that, Kijapa died. The master ordered him to bury it in the dust heap. That night he fell asleep without a scrap of bad conscience. for his ungrateful treatment of the amazing gazelle to whom he really owed everything. And in the morning when he woke up he was once again a ragged beggar in his old hut. When he was hungry he had to go out to the dust heap to scratch for some scraps of food. The village children mocked him and said, "Alhamdani, where have you been? You have been away so long we thought you were dead. But I am pleased to say that the sultan's daughter, who had a good heart and was grateful for all her good fortune in life, lived in the house in comfort, peace, and happiness until the end of her face.

Or have you ever shouted in the mountains and been surprised when your own voice shouted right back? Well, I am here with a Greek myth that unveils the mystery behind the very first Narcissus flower and introduces you to a unique girl named Ekko who had a peculiar habit of only repeating the last words she heard. There was this lad named Narcissus. At 16, he stood at the crossroads of youth and adulthood. And my, he was a good-looking boy. The gods had blessed him with such good looks that flowers would twist and twirl to watch him wander by. And even the breezes couldn't help but spread tales of his captivating charm. An old and insightful sear. Tyresius once made a curious prediction about him. He'll live a long life unless he comes face to face with himself. Quite a riddle, right? What do you think he meant by that? After all, mirrors were not even invented back then. So, how could he come face to face with himself? We shall see. On a sun-kissed day, while exploring the meadows, Narcissus discovered a pond with water so clear. It mirrored the world above. As he peered into its depths, he saw a radiant face staring back. "Who might this be?" he thought. It was love at first sight. The face was so beautiful that he could help falling for it. Deep, deep in love. Yet every time he reached out to touch the mesmerizing face, it would ripple away. Day after day, he sat by the pond, completely entranced. The face in the water smiled, cried, and laughed just as he did. "Why won't you join me?" He often wondered, not realizing he was admiring his own reflection, hidden in the shadows. The nymph Eko watched with a heavy heart, once a chatterbox. Now the goddess Juno had cursed to only echo the last words she heard. That's why she was called Echo, right? She wished to call out to the beautiful boy, but all she could do was repeat his size. When he lamented, "Oh, I'm in love," she'd echo. in love. And when he said, "I'm so smitten," she would echo back, "So smitten." But here's the twist. Narcissus wasn't talking to Ekko. When he declared his love, he was enamored by his own reflection. And when he heard Ekko's reply, he believed his watery twin was responding. And poor Ekko thought that he had fallen in love with her. But he hadn't even noticed the poor nymph. He was totally absorbed in his own reflection. I know it sounds unbelievable that a man could be so vain and totally in love with himself, but this is a true story. Yet his every attempt to kiss his reflection only ended in ripples and wet cheeks. With each passing day, Narcissus grew more fawn, wishing his reflection could step out and they could embrace. Ekko watching from afar would echo his wishes. Adding to the confusion, the boy was so lovesick for his own reflection that he could not sleep. He stopped eating. He did not drink. He hardly breathed. One fateful evening, bathed in the glow of a setting sun. Narcissus whispered his heart-wrenching farewell. Goodbye, my love. Goodbye. An echo, her voice quivering with sorrow. echoed. Goodbye. By sunrise, where the heartbroken boy once sat, a radiant flower blossomed, its white petals guarding a golden heart, it was christened Narcissus, a tribute to the boy who was lost in his own beauty. So, next time you spot a Narcissus flower or hear an echo, remember this tale of a boy lost in his own reflection and of a nymph whose love remained unspoken. What a mesmerizing tale, right? Narcissus's story is an age-old reminder about the dangers of being too self-absorbed. And it's thanks to him that we call someone who thinks too highly of themselves a yacha narcissist. If you meet one of these people, don't be like Ekko and just repeat back everything they want you to say. Narcissists can be very controlling. If you can, avoid. That's my advice. Next time you see a narcissus flower or hear an echo in the mountains, remember this tale and the importance of loving others and not just ourselves.
